name: Neckmaxxing / neck training

card.summary: Building a thicker neck to improve frame and jaw proportions; discussed with ratio targets that no published study validates.
card.note: Community guides involve loaded neck exercises; ratio targets are forum conventions.

quick.overview:
Neckmaxxing is the practice of training the neck muscles to make the neck thicker, which proponents say improves overall proportions and the look of the jaw. It is described on looksmax.org as a softmaxx.

Forum posts propose ideal ratios, for example neck width compared with jaw (bigonial) width near 1:1, and share training guides.
quick.mechanism: Neck exercises load the muscles around the cervical spine, with the sternocleidomastoid named in forum guides as the muscle that thickens the neck from the front. Proponents say a thicker neck makes a narrow head and jaw look more balanced with the body.
quick.risks: Loaded neck exercises sit near the cervical spine. One forum guide calls neck work one of the most dangerous softmaxxes. No clinical studies of neckmaxxing for appearance were found.

lead: Neckmaxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of training the neck muscles to build a thicker, more defined neck. Practitioners say a wider neck gives the head and jaw a stronger frame, adds to a masculine, powerful look and balances a broad jaw or shoulders, and forum members describe it as one of the more visible changes available from lifting.[1][2][6]

Forum guides describe neck curls, extensions and side raises, sometimes with a towel or a weight plate, plus slow bodyweight variations that emphasise stretch.[6][7] Community posts give proportion targets: a neck-to-bigonial (jaw width) ratio of about 0.95 to 1, a neck matching the widest part of the face, and in one thread a neck width-to-height ratio near 1.35.[1][2] These are community conventions rather than published standards.

Outside looksmaxxing, neck strengthening is studied in sport and rehabilitation. A randomised trial in healthy women found that ten weeks of neck training increased the cross-sectional area of the neck muscles, with larger gains when resistance work was combined with proprioceptive exercises.[4] Consumer health writing also lists flexion, extension, lateral flexion and rotation exercises and says a muscular neck looks strong, especially when flexed.[9]

angle.text: Training the neck builds the muscles around it, which makes the neck look wider from the front and side. Looksmaxxing guides pair this with jaw and shoulder proportions, saying a thicker neck supports a more masculine outline.[1][2]

paras: Forum guides describe adding neck exercises such as curls and extensions to a lifting routine. One author calls the neck among the most dangerous yet rewarding softmaxxes and claims it could add about 0.5 PSL points.[2] PSL is a community rating scale for looks and is not a validated measure.

A thread titled as a guide lists the benefits as a thicker and stronger neck that can go with the physique, improved posture over time and what the author calls a 'high T' look; it demonstrates two exercises done with a towel over the head.[6] Replies in that thread suggest slow tempo and stretch can produce growth even without added weight.[6]

Posters compare necks to celebrity examples and discuss proportions with the head and jaw, saying that people with a small or narrow skull may already be proportional while those with a wide skull would need to build neck size.[1] A guide on the sternocleidomastoid describes keeping the neck 'packed' during curls.[2] Before and after posts show results of neck training alongside other changes.[3]

Common questions on looksmax.org include how often to train, whether training one side more will leave the neck asymmetrical, and what to change when two months of training shows no results.[7][8] One thread title argues neck training is important for people who have a wider face and better jawline but still a thin neck.[10]

A ten-week randomised pilot trial in 26 healthy women reported neck muscle cross-sectional area increases in all three muscle groups measured, between 1.5 and 12.9 percent in a resistance-only group and 18.9 to 32.3 percent in a resistance plus proprioceptive group.[4] A randomised study of 180 women with chronic neck pain found neck strength rose most in a high-intensity isometric group, with gains continuing across 12 months.[5]

In sports medicine, a systematic review and Delphi consensus examined neck training to reduce head acceleration events in sport.[11] Healthline's guide to a thicker neck lists exercises and says a muscular neck looks strong, and that neck exercises can ease tension and help prevent injury.[9]

Health writing advises stopping any neck exercise that causes pain and moving slowly with good posture.[9] One looksmax.org thread title raises the possibility that neck training can cause sleep apnoea,[12] while Healthline notes that excess neck fat, rather than muscle, may raise sleep apnoea risk.[9]

No studies found of neck training for facial or physique appearance in the looksmaxxing sense. Related studies of neck training include a randomised pilot trial measuring neck muscle size after resistance and proprioceptive training,[4] a 12-month randomised study of strength training for chronic neck pain,[5] a Delphi consensus on neck training in sport[11] and trials of corticomotor effects of neck training.[13]

lore.intro: Neckmaxxing threads on looksmax.org mix anatomy, ratio targets, training guides and progress photos.[1][2][7]

claims.claim: A neck about as wide as the jaw is ideal.
claims.believers: Posters give ratios of about 0.95 to 1 neck to bigonial width and cite celebrity examples.[1][2]
claims.experts: No published studies were found on neck width ratios and perceived attractiveness.

claims.claim: Neck training can add notable rating points to overall looks.
claims.believers: One guide claims about 0.5 PSL points.[2]
claims.experts: PSL is a forum scale. No studies measure the effect of neck training on rated attractiveness.

claims.claim: Neck muscles respond to training and can be built.
claims.believers: Posters share before and after pictures and training logs.[3][8]
claims.experts: A randomised trial found neck muscle cross-sectional area increased after ten weeks of training in healthy women.[4]

claims.claim: A thick neck goes with a high-testosterone look and better posture.
claims.believers: A guide thread says a thicker neck goes with the physique and improves posture over time.[6]
claims.experts: Expert guidance on neck thickness for appearance was not found; studies examine strength and pain rather than posture or hormone-related appearance.[5]

claims.claim: Neck training is risky or can cause sleep apnoea.
claims.believers: A guide calls it one of the most dangerous softmaxxes, and one thread title claims it can cause sleep apnoea.[2][12]
claims.experts: Healthline advises stopping painful exercises and notes excess neck fat may raise sleep apnoea risk.[9] No injury data on neckmaxxing were found.
